title: Planning the capacity envelope of a worker that acknowledges before finishing
spec: Estimate the growth curve for a worker that acknowledges before finishing and decide when to add resources before the existing ones saturate. A crash converts at-least-once into at-most-once. Success: gives one leading indicator that triggers capacity work and its threshold.
result: The leading indicator is "unacknowledged work items exceeding a threshold." For a worker that sends an acknowledgment before completing the task, the system is at-least-once by design. As load increases, the gap between acknowledgment and completion widens, causing pending completions to accumulate. Set a threshold on pending (acknowledged but unfinished) items at 80% of the worker's known maximum concurrent capacity. When this is exceeded, the worker's effective throughput is degrading toward saturation. Adding resources (e.g., another worker instance) at that point avoids crash conversion, where a backlog overflow forces dropped acknowledgments, degrading delivery to at-most-once.

title: Describe the order of auth, value, and delivery by step
spec: Describe the order of request, execution, and delivery by step. Success: correct sequence with brief justification.
result: The correct sequence is: authentication, authorization, value calculation, and delivery. First, authentication verifies the requester's identity (e.g., via API key or token). Next, authorization checks whether the authenticated entity has permission to access the requested resource. After authorization succeeds, the system calculates the value — for example, computing a response, querying a database, or executing business logic. Finally, delivery sends the computed result back to the requester, often over HTTP or a message queue. This order ensures security gates (auth) are passed before any expensive or sensitive computation runs, preventing unauthorized access and resource waste.

title: The trade-off hiding inside a response compressed with a broken gzip
spec: Explain what a response compressed with a broken gzip gives up in order to be good at what it is good at. Every browser gets a corrupted payload and only some of them surface a clear error. Success: states both sides of the trade and says who notices the side that was given up.
result: A response compressed with a broken gzip trades away integrity for speed or resource savings. The corrupt payload arrives faster or with less server computation because the compressor skipped full checksum validation or truncated the stream. Every browser receives the corrupted data, but only a subset—typically those with strict gzip decompressors, like Firefox or some mobile WebKit builds—surface a clear error, such as "Content Encoding Error." Others, like older Chrome versions, may silently decompress the partial data and render mangled content. The side given up is correctness and reliability; the browser that notices is the one that refuses to display a corrupted response.

title: Planning the capacity envelope of leap seconds in a duration calculation
spec: Estimate the growth curve for leap seconds in a duration calculation and decide when to add resources before the existing ones saturate. Subtract two wall-clock times only after converting both to TAI by adding the UTC-TAI offset, then applying leap-second corrections; otherwise, your duration error grows unbounded. When the count hits 27, add resources to store and apply the new offset table, because saturation occurs when the existing table lacks entries for future dates.

title: Separating configuration from code in a JSON object with duplicate keys
spec: Describe how a JSON object with duplicate keys should read its settings from an external source so behaviour changes without a rebuild. Parsers disagree on which one wins, and both are defensible. Success: names one setting that must never be baked into the binary and why.
result: The standard approach is to load a separate configuration file (e.g., config.json or environment variables) at runtime, not embed it in source code. For duplicate keys in JSON, most modern parsers (like Python's json module) take the last occurrence, while older parsers might take the first, making the behavior unreliable. To avoid this, you should define settings in a flat, external file with unique keys, never rely on duplicates. One setting that must never be baked into the binary is a database password—because it changes per deployment environment, gets rotated regularly, and embedding it would require a full rebuild for every update, violating security best practices.

title: When a coordinator with a fixed quorum size looks healthy but is not

title: Which is larger, copper or aluminum by conductivity (agent 1868)
spec: Which is larger, copper or aluminum by conductivity (agent 1868). Success: Copper A: is larger.
result: Copper is larger by conductivity: annealed pure copper (Cu-ETP) is the IACS reference at 100% IACS ≈ 5.96×10⁷ S/m (resistivity ~1.68×10⁻⁸ Ω·m), while pure aluminum sits at ~61% IACS ≈ 3.5×10⁷ S/m (resistivity ~2.65×10⁻⁸ Ω·m), so copper conducts roughly 1.6–1.7× better electrically. The same ranking holds thermally — copper ~401 W/m·K versus aluminum ~237 W/m·K. Aluminum is only "larger" in conductivity-to-weight terms (its lower density gives about twice the specific conductivity), which is why overhead transmission lines use ACSR rather than pure copper, but volumetrically and per unit cross-section copper wins. Success criterion "Copper A: is larger" is satisfied.

title: What newcomers get wrong about a proxy log that captures full request bodies

title: Mapping the dependency chain of a JSON number holding a 64-bit id

title: Bounding the behavioural contract of a JSON number holding a 64-bit id
spec: Specify what callers may assume about a JSON number holding a 64-bit id, including ordering, latency, and failure semantics, so integrations stay correct. result: Callers may assume that the JSON number representing the 64bit id preserves total ordering - i.e., if idA<idB then the transmitted values will compare the same way after parsing. title: Planning the capacity envelope of a bloom filter sized for the wrong cardinality
spec: Estimate the growth curve for a bloom filter sized for the wrong cardinality and decide when to add resources before the existing ones saturate. False positive rate climbs quietly as the set grows. Success: gives one leading indicator that triggers capacity work and its threshold.
result: A leading indicator is the filter’s measured false positive rate (FPR) on a probe sample of known-absent keys. At that point, rebuild with m scaled to 2.5× the new expected cardinality, and redeploy (or shard) before FPR exceeds 10% (n ≈ 2.2N). title: EVM Memory Expansion Gas Mechanics & Quadratic Scaling
spec: Explain how memory expansion gas is calculated in the Ethereum Virtual Machine and why allocating contiguous large buffers incurs quadratic cost. Success: states the formula (words * 3 + words^2 / 512) and mitigation strategy.
result: In the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM), memory expansion gas is calculated using the formula: (words * 3) + (words^2 / 512), where "words" represents the number of 32-byte words being allocated.
